title: Suder v. Commissioner
subject: Qualified Research Expenses
summary: Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, is a U.S. Tax Court R&D tax credit case under IRC § 41 involving Estech Systems, Inc., a Texas S corporation, and its shareholders. The Court held that 11 of 12 sample projects were qualified research and upheld Cohan-based wage estimates, but found $30.67 million of CEO pay unreasonable under IRC § 174(e).

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
1.1 Factual Genesis and Taxpayer Claim Architecture

In Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, the United States Tax Court adjudicated a landmark dispute concerning the eligibility, substantiation, and valuation of federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credits claimed under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41 for the 2004 through 2007 tax years. The underlying research activities were conducted by Estech Systems, Inc. (ESI), a Texas-based S corporation founded in 1987 by petitioner Eric Suder out of his garage after his former employer, Candela Electronics, went out of business. Initially generating short-term cash flow by purchasing surplus Candela private branch exchange (PBX) units negotiated from Radio Shack for cents on the dollar, testing them, repackaging them, and reselling them at a profit, Mr. Suder recognized that limited PBX supply required a transition into original equipment manufacturing and software development. In 1988, he hired his first employee, and by 1989 he designed ESI's first proprietary product—an embedded system designated "Phone Bill" that approximated long-distance telephone call costs using geographic bands rather than complex rate tables. By the 2004–2007 period at issue, ESI operated with approximately 125 total employees, including roughly 40 specialized hardware, firmware, call-processing, and graphical user interface (GUI) engineers developing integrated telephone hardware and software systems for small and midsize businesses.

During the tax years at issue, ESI was wholly owned by two shareholders residing in Texas: Eric Suder, who served as Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and owned 90% of ESI's stock, and Douglas Boyd, who served as President and Chief Operating Officer (COO) and owned the remaining 10%. Building on an R&D tax credit study that the external tax advisory firm Alliantgroup had performed for ESI's 1999–2002 tax years—after which SVP Harvey Wende computed ESI's QREs for 2004–2007 himself, while Deloitte & Touche separately audited ESI's financial statements—ESI claimed substantial qualified research expenses (QREs) across 76 distinct product development projects undertaken between 2004 and 2007. Because ESI elected pass-through taxation as an S corporation, the resulting IRC § 41 research credits flowed through proportionately to the individual federal income tax returns of its shareholders, with Mr. Suder claiming flow-through credits exceeding $440,000 each year ($445,987, $440,306, $454,526, and $442,557 for 2004–2007) and Mr. Boyd claiming credits exceeding $46,000 each year ($46,748, $46,624, $48,870, and $48,378 for 2004–2007).

The quantitative composition of ESI's claimed QREs was heavily weighted toward in-house employee wages, which represented more than 95% of the company's claimed QREs, while research supplies ($236,846 for 2004, $164,241 for 2005, $109,816 for 2006, and $182,711 for 2007) and modest contract research expenses ($29,915 for 2004, $15,531 for 2005, $7,755 for 2006, and $10,316 for 2007) made up the remainder (less than 5%). Within the wage QRE category, Harvey Wende—ESI's Senior Vice President of Product Operations from 2004 to 2006 and Senior Vice President of Product Development in 2007—formulated annual employee time-allocation spreadsheets estimating the percentage of time each employee devoted to qualified services. Mr. Wende assigned a 100% allocation to himself and to the vast majority of ESI's engineers, product managers, and product testers, reducing the percentage only for personnel who performed routine maintenance work more than sporadically. He further assigned a 5% to 10% allocation for quality control and shipping personnel, and a 75% allocation for Mr. Suder. Because Mr. Suder received total W-2 compensation of $8,674,815 in 2004, $10,954,175 in 2005, $10,548,022 in 2006, and $10,502,584 in 2007, his 75% wage allocation alone constituted roughly two-thirds of ESI's total dollar amount of claimed wage QREs for each of the tax years under examination.
1.2 The Internal Revenue Service Challenge

Following a comprehensive audit examination, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) mailed statutory notices of deficiency on March 19, 2009, and January 25, 2010, to both Mr. Suder and Mr. Boyd, disallowing in their entirety the research tax credits they claimed for 2004–2005 and 2006–2007, respectively, while also determining 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a). To manage the complexity of litigating 76 separate engineering initiatives, the parties selected 12 of the 76 projects and stipulated that those 12 projects were representative of the entire pool for purposes of determining whether ESI performed "qualified research" within the meaning of IRC § 41(d).

The Commissioner mounted an aggressive, multi-faceted challenge across five legal and evidentiary fronts. First, while not disputing that the 12 representative projects satisfied the technological information and business component tests, the IRS contended that they failed the Section 174 and process of experimentation tests of IRC § 41(d), arguing—principally through its expert, Dr. Charles Jackson—that the projects were routine or merely matched products already offered by industry leaders such as Avaya and Cisco, that ESI's evidence showed only the uncertainty inherent in any large development effort (deadlines, lack of resources, unexpected delays, and human error), that ESI chose among design alternatives by applying engineering know-how, publicly available knowledge, or committee decisions rather than a process of experimentation, and that debugging of products already used by customers was excluded as research after commercial production under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A). Second, the IRS argued that ESI failed to substantiate its QREs because it maintained no contemporaneous time-tracking system linking employee hours to individual business components, asserting that Mr. Wende's annual percentage estimates—which the IRS also argued he lacked the tax or accounting background to make—failed to provide the requisite "nexus" between claimed expenses and qualified research activities. Third, the Commissioner challenged the wage allocations themselves—including the 75% allocation for Mr. Suder—as unsubstantiated, arguing that the facts were "directly analogous" to Shami v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-78, in which the Tax Court had rejected as non-credible the testimony offered to support the wage allocations claimed for two executives of Farouk Systems, Inc. Fourth, the IRS challenged the reasonableness of Mr. Suder's multi-million-dollar wages as QREs under the statutory reasonableness limitation of IRC § 174(e), with its compensation expert, Dr. Khalid Hafiz, concluding that reasonable wages for Mr. Suder should not exceed upper-quartile values of $1,018,185 to $1,131,436 per year. Finally, the IRS asserted that the taxpayers were liable for 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a) because they failed to establish reasonable cause and good faith under IRC § 6664(c).
1.3 Governing United States Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The legal dispute in Suder is governed by the interconnected statutory architecture of IRC §§ 41, 174, 6001, 6662, and 6664, alongside the corresponding Treasury Regulations and foundational United States judicial precedents. Because tax credits are a matter of legislative grace and the Commissioner's determinations in a deficiency notice are presumed correct under Tax Court Rule 142(a) and Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111, 115 (1933), the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proving entitlement to the claimed credits under INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79, 84 (1992), and New Colonial Ice Co. v. Helvering, 292 U.S. 435, 440 (1934). Under the regular credit calculation of IRC § 41(a)(1), a taxpayer is entitled to a credit equal to 20% of the excess of the taxpayer's total QREs for the credit year over the "base amount." Pursuant to IRC § 41(c)(1)–(3), the base amount is defined as the product of the taxpayer's "fixed-base percentage"—generally the lesser of 16% or the ratio that the taxpayer's aggregate QREs bear to aggregate gross receipts during a statutory historical base period—and the average annual gross receipts of the taxpayer for the four taxable years preceding the credit year. However, IRC § 41(c)(2) imposes a strict statutory floor mandating that in no event may the base amount be less than 50% of the QREs for the credit year. Alternatively, taxpayers may elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC § 41(c)(4), which provides a credit equal to 14% of the excess of credit-year QREs over 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years, or 6% of credit-year QREs if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years (ESI itself did not use the ASC; it computed its regular credit using a fixed-base percentage of 16%, the statutory maximum, for each year at issue).

To generate eligible QREs under either calculation method, the underlying activities must satisfy the four-part statutory test for "qualified research" codified in IRC § 41(d)(1), which must be applied separately to each "business component"—defined under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. First, under the Section 174 Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), the expenditures must be eligible to be treated as expenses under IRC § 174. Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures satisfy this threshold if they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense, meaning the activities are intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a product or process, or the appropriate design of that product or process, based on information available to the taxpayer at the outset of the activities. Second, under the Technological Information Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, which requires that the process of experimentation fundamentally rely on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

Third, under the Business Component Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), the taxpayer must intend that the application of the discovered technological information be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), "substantially all" of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation that relates to a "qualified purpose." Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5) defines a process of experimentation as a systematic evaluative process aligned with the scientific method that involves identifying the technical uncertainty, identifying one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and conducting a methodical series of trials—such as modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error—to test, analyze, and refine those alternatives. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement is satisfied only if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities for a given business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Furthermore, IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) defines a "qualified purpose" as research conducted for the purpose of developing a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, whereas IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) expressly excludes any research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. If an overall business component fails the four-part test, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) mandates the application of the "shrinking-back rule," instructing that the four requirements be applied to progressively smaller subsets of elements of the business component until either a qualifying subset is reached or the most basic element of the product or software fails to satisfy the test.

Once qualified research is established at the business-component level, IRC § 41(b)(1) restricts QREs to the sum of "in-house research expenses" and "contract research expenses." In-house research expenses comprise wages (as defined in IRC § 3401(a)) paid or incurred for "qualified services"—which IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) defines as engaging in qualified research, or engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of research activities which constitute qualified research—and amounts paid or incurred for tangible "supplies" (other than land or depreciable property) used in the conduct of qualified research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)–(ii). Under the flush language of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), as implemented by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), if "substantially all" (at least 80%) of an employee's services during a taxable year consist of qualified services, then 100% of that employee's wages for the taxable year qualify as QREs. Contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3) equal 65% of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for qualified research, provided under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) that the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the research, requires the research to be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and mandates that the taxpayer bear the economic expense even if the research is not successful. Crucially, IRC § 174(e) imposes an overarching valuation limitation across all research expenditures, dictating that Section 174 applies to a research or experimental expenditure only to the extent that the amount thereof is reasonable under the circumstances.
1.4 The Tax Court's Final Holding

Following a three-week special trial session in Dallas, Texas (July 2013) generating more than 3,500 pages of testimony and more than 170,000 pages of evidentiary exhibits, Judge Vasquez issued a comprehensive memorandum opinion yielding a split doctrinal outcome that paired broad validation of incremental engineering activities with a severe downward adjustment to executive compensation QREs. On the threshold issue of project eligibility, the Tax Court held that 11 of the 12 stipulated projects satisfied all four requirements of IRC § 41(d) (Arcadia, Clark Kent, Rio Grande, Mad Max, Express FSII, Suzuki, Phoenix, Pony, DLC0, DLC82, and IVC1212). The Court found that ESI followed a methodical, systematic product development process—moving from macro-feasibility brainstorming to multi-iteration functional and design specifications, hardware schematics, physical PCB prototyping, firmware and software coding, and multi-stage alpha and beta testing—that satisfied the process of experimentation test. Rejecting the IRS's contention that ESI merely chose among design alternatives by applying engineering know-how, publicly available knowledge, or committee decisions—and finding no persuasive distinction between principles of engineering and "engineering know-how"—the Court articulated a foundational principle: "Neither section 41 nor the regulations thereunder require taxpayers to 'reinvent the wheel'". Conversely, the Court disqualified the Chameleon project, holding that incorporating a third-party skinning tool merely to alter the aesthetic "look and feel" of a user interface failed the qualified purpose test of IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) and fell squarely within the statutory exclusion for style, taste, or cosmetic design factors under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B), even though Chameleon had satisfied the Section 174 test; applying the parties' stipulation, the Court therefore found that 91.67% (eleven-twelfths) of the 76 projects constituted qualified research.

Regarding the substantiation of wage QREs, the Tax Court rejected the IRS's argument that ESI's claim must fail for lack of project-specific time-tracking "nexus." Applying the estimation rule of Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), the Court held that SVP Harvey Wende's credible, detailed testimony (given over four days on the witness stand) based on his intimate familiarity with ESI's business and employees, corroborated by the credible testimony of petitioners' other witnesses, several of the Commissioner's own witnesses, and the documentary evidence in the record, provided a reasonable basis to uphold ESI's employee wage allocation percentages, including the 75% allocation assigned to Mr. Suder for his hands-on ideation, specification review, and alpha testing. However, in a major victory for the Commissioner, the Court held that Mr. Suder's actual wages ($8.67 million to $10.95 million per year) were unreasonable under IRC § 174(e). Evaluating the competing expert valuations of Brent Longnecker (for the taxpayers) and Dr. Khalid Hafiz (for the IRS), the Court accepted Mr. Longnecker's 90th-percentile calculations for base salary, annual incentive, and long-term incentive, but completely disallowed Mr. Longnecker's $8.67 million to $10.17 million annual "royalty" component. Consequently, the Court reduced Mr. Suder's reasonable compensation eligible for the 75% QRE allocation to $2,366,090 for 2004, $2,439,174 for 2005, $2,558,098 for 2006, and $2,643,907 for 2007, finding $30,672,327 of his total wages for 2004–2007 unreasonable and reducing his wage QREs (at the 75% allocation) to $1,774,568 for 2004, $1,829,381 for 2005, $1,918,574 for 2006, and $1,982,930 for 2007. The Court upheld ESI's claimed supply QREs—which were tracked in a dedicated R&D general ledger account for prototype components and fabrication—and allowed the contract research expenses paid to two law firms for patent research and prosecution. Finally, the Court relieved Mr. Suder and Mr. Boyd of all accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a) pursuant to the reasonable cause and good faith exception of IRC § 6664(c), holding that, as experts in telephone systems rather than tax matters who had hired Alliantgroup, reasonably entrusted the QRE computations to SVP Wende, and consulted their longtime CPA, Margaret Rogers, in setting their wages, they acted with reasonable cause and in good faith—under an honest and reasonable misunderstanding of the law—in navigating "one of the most complicated provisions in the Code."
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

While Suder v. Commissioner is frequently cited by tax practitioners for its taxpayer-favorable holdings regarding incremental engineering and Cohan wage estimates, a rigorous legal audit of the opinion reveals severe structural, technical, and evidentiary failures in the taxpayer's claim. These deficiencies not only caused the outright disqualification of the Chameleon project and the disallowance of more than $30.67 million in executive compensation, but also forced the taxpayers to endure an examination and litigation process spanning more than five years from the first notice of deficiency (March 19, 2009) to the opinion (filed October 1, 2014), including a three-week trial with more than 3,500 pages of testimony and more than 170,000 pages of exhibits. An examination of each core failure illustrates the precise statutory traps that undermine R&D tax credit claims in the United States.
2.1 Disqualification of the Chameleon Project: Failure of Qualified Purpose and the IRC Section 41(d)(3)(B) Cosmetic Exclusion

The most direct technical project failure in Suder occurred in the Chameleon project, which was the sole business component among the 12 stipulated sample projects to be completely disqualified by the Tax Court. To understand why Chameleon failed while the other 11 hardware and software projects succeeded, one must contrast the technical objectives and engineering uncertainties of the qualifying projects against the statutory mandate of IRC § 41(d)(3), as detailed in the project comparison below.

body.text: In the 11 qualifying projects, ESI demonstrated that its engineers confronted genuine technological uncertainties regarding capability, method, or appropriate design that directly enhanced system functionality, performance, reliability, or quality. Furthermore, distinguishing adverse appellate precedents such as United Stationers, Inc. v. United States and Norwest Corp. v. Commissioner—where the taxpayers modified existing software programs (a purchased commercial package in United Stationers and the taxpayer's own money transfer system in Norwest) and faced business risks but no technical uncertainty—the Tax Court emphasized that ESI's projects involved the development of new software—written in assembly language, C, and higher-level GUI code—that was layered on top of newly developed hardware or added features or functionality to ESI's proprietary phone systems, none of it operating as a stand-alone program. In stark contrast, the Chameleon project was initiated to integrate a third-party "skinning" software tool into ESI's Visual Interface Phone (VIP) software suite. The sole objective of the project was to alter the "look and feel" of the VIP user interface by giving end users the ability to modify screen colors, typography fonts, button shapes, and button sizes. During trial, ESI's senior vice president Harvey Wende credibly testified—likening the project to giving a person the choice of a paint color on an automobile—that the Chameleon project did not actually alter, enhance, or improve the underlying functionality of the VIP software suite.

This admission proved legally fatal under the fourth prong of the qualified research test. Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation that relates to a "qualified purpose." IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) strictly confines a qualified purpose to research undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that improves the function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component. Conversely, IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) establishes an absolute statutory exclusion dictating that research shall not be treated as conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors.

From a technical tax advisory perspective, ESI committed two compounding errors regarding Chameleon. First, the taxpayer conflated technical integration effort with a qualified statutory purpose. Software developers routinely encounter programming challenges when integrating third-party graphical libraries or skinning APIs into proprietary codebases. However, even if an engineer experiences uncertainty regarding the method of coding a visual skinning hook—thereby satisfying the Section 174 uncertainty test and the Technological Information test, as the Court actually found for Chameleon, stating that ESI had resolved the technical uncertainty of incorporating the third-party skinning tool—the activity still fails IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) if the end purpose of that code is purely aesthetic or cosmetic under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B). Similarly, to the extent that any project activity consists merely of routine bug fixing on an already commercially available product after commercial production has commenced, such post-production maintenance is statutorily excluded from qualified research. Second, the opinion contains no shrinking-back analysis for Chameleon, and nothing in the record identified a functional subset of the project to which the Court could have applied the "shrinking-back rule" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). With ESI treating the entire Chameleon skinning project as a whole, and with Mr. Wende confirming that it did not change the VIP suite's functionality, the Court treated the project as entirely cosmetic (no functional subcomponent—such as re-architecting the VIP client's graphical rendering pipeline—appears in the record), resulting in the disqualification of Chameleon.
2.2 The IRC Section 174(e) Reasonable Compensation Failure: Disguised S-Corporation Distributions and Flawed Royalty Valuations

The single largest monetary disallowance in Suder stemmed from the taxpayer's failure to satisfy IRC § 174(e), which mandates that research or experimental expenditures are eligible for tax-favored treatment only to the extent that the amounts are "reasonable under the circumstances". In Suder, the Tax Court addressed the intersection of IRC § 174(e) and IRC § 41 wage QREs for the first time, expressly describing the issue as one of first impression in the Tax Court, exposing a pervasive structural vulnerability among closely held S corporations and partnerships.

Because S corporations are pass-through entities not subject to entity-level federal income tax, shareholder-executives ordinarily face an incentive to minimize W-2 wages to reduce FICA and Medicare payroll taxes. However, when an S corporation claims the IRC § 41 research credit, that tax incentive reverses completely: pass-through dividend distributions do not constitute "wages" under IRC § 3401(a) and cannot be claimed as QREs, whereas W-2 wages paid to shareholder-employees for qualified services generate a lucrative, dollar-for-dollar flow-through tax credit. In ESI's case, Mr. Suder (90% shareholder) and Mr. Boyd (10% shareholder) received massive W-2 compensation packages consisting of a base salary and bonuses based on factors that included ESI's growth, overall value, and cashflow.

The evidentiary record revealed five glaring defects that destroyed the taxpayers' position that Mr. Suder's $8.67 million to $10.95 million annual compensation was reasonable in whole. First, the compensation was paid in direct proportion to stockholdings. Mr. Suder received total wages of $8,674,815 for 2004, $10,954,175 for 2005, $10,548,022 for 2006, and $10,502,584 for 2007, whereas Mr. Boyd, ESI's second most highly compensated employee, received wages of $934,919 for 2004, $1,354,553 for 2005, $1,308,926 for 2006, and $1,304,776 for 2007. The Tax Court observed that their wages moved up and down in tandem and maintained a ratio of approximately 9.28:1 in 2004, 8.09:1 in 2005, 8.06:1 in 2006, and 8.05:1 in 2007—ratios roughly proportionate to their 9:1 (90% versus 10%) ownership interests in ESI. Under settled federal tax law, ostensible compensation paid to majority shareholders in proportion to their stockholdings requires close judicial scrutiny as a disguised distribution of corporate earnings.

Second, Mr. Suder's wages were wildly disproportionate to ESI's corporate net income, equaling approximately 4.5 times, 6.0 times, 5.5 times, and 5.5 times ESI's ordinary business income for 2004, 2005, 2006, and 2007, respectively, which, the Court held, suggested that his compensation was, at least in part, unreasonable. Third, the evidentiary record contained zero numerical breakdown of Mr. Suder's or Mr. Boyd's base salaries versus their cash-flow bonuses for any of the years at issue. Fourth, no evidence demonstrated that Mr. Suder's compensation surge during 2004–2007 was tied to his contribution to R&D. Whereas Mr. Suder worked 60 to 80 hours per week during ESI's early years, during 2004–2007 he worked a variable schedule averaging only 20 to 30 hours per week, devoting substantial time to unaffiliated non-profit organizations in the Dallas area. Moreover, although Mr. Suder was named as an inventor on 13 patents over his career, all of those original patent applications either predated or postdated the 2004–2007 tax years (with only a single patent reissuance application filed on June 3, 2005), yet his wages in 2004–2007 were significantly higher than in prior years, notwithstanding that he was not named as an inventor on any new patent applications filed from 2004 to 2007.

Fifth, the taxpayers' expert witness valuation suffered from fatal methodological flaws. To defend Mr. Suder's compensation, the taxpayers retained compensation expert Brent Longnecker, who opined that reasonable compensation at the 90th percentile of comparable companies totaled $11,035,735 for 2004, $11,321,086 for 2005, $12,179,498 for 2006, and $12,814,798 for 2007. However, roughly 78–79% of Mr. Longnecker's proposed reasonable compensation consisted of hypothetical "gross revenue royalties" totaling $8,669,645 in 2004, $8,881,913 in 2005, $9,621,400 in 2006, and $10,170,891 in 2007. The Tax Court completely rejected Mr. Longnecker's royalty component on both evidentiary and substantive legal grounds, noting first and foremost petitioners' admission in their reply brief that Mr. Suder had never been compensated through royalty payments of any kind. As an evidentiary matter, Mr. Longnecker was not an expert in intellectual property valuation, relied on unverified royalty rates (18.75%, 22.50%, and 23.75% for the 75th, 90th, and 95th percentiles) provided over the telephone roughly two years earlier by a "Dr. Esber" whose background he could not recall, and multiplied those royalty rates by ESI's overall gross revenues without knowing what percentage of gross revenue was actually attributable to patented technology. As a matter of substantive tax law, royalties paid for intellectual property rights do not constitute IRC § 3401(a) wages paid for personal services rendered by an employee and are ineligible as QREs. By excising the royalty component while accepting Mr. Longnecker's 90th-percentile figures for base salary, annual incentive, and long-term incentive—categories that both Mr. Longnecker and IRS expert Dr. Khalid Hafiz agreed belonged in a reasonable package, although Dr. Hafiz advocated a lower upper-quartile ceiling of $1,018,185 to $1,131,436—the Court found $30,672,327 (75.4%) of Mr. Suder's total wages across the four-year period unreasonable under IRC § 174(e), as quantified in the table below.

body.text: 2.3 Evidentiary Deficiencies in Contemporaneous Time-Tracking, Project-to-Expense Nexus, and the "Substantially All" Threshold

A third foundational deficiency in Suder—one that the IRS attacked at trial as a lack of "nexus" and that carries severe risk under contemporary United States judicial precedent—was that ESI's wage QREs rested on annual percentage allocations rather than on contemporaneous time records linking employee hours to specific research projects and specific experimental activities. Rather than relying on hours logged by project code and activity phase, ESI relied on an annual estimation methodology executed by SVP Harvey Wende, who modeled his spreadsheets on those Alliantgroup had prepared for 1999–2002 and, for employees he did not know well, spoke with them or their supervisors before making allocations. Each year, Mr. Wende used the prior year's Excel spreadsheet allocation as a starting point, considered whether an employee's role had changed since the prior year, and assigned a single annual percentage allocation to each individual. For Mr. Suder, Mr. Wende testified that he believed an 80% allocation was appropriate to reflect Mr. Suder's role as the creative genius behind product development at ESI, but "in a measure of conservatism," he decided to allocate 75% of Mr. Suder's time to qualified services specifically to avoid triggering the 80% "substantially all" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2).

Although the Tax Court ultimately rescued ESI's wage allocations under the Cohan doctrine by crediting Mr. Wende's oral testimony and declining to require project-by-project wage nexus, relying on Suder to justify non-contemporaneous spreadsheet estimates in modern tax practice is a perilous strategic miscalculation for three interconnected reasons. First, the evidentiary cost of invoking Cohan in Suder was extraordinary: the Tax Court permitted ESI to estimate its wage QREs only after a three-week trial featuring four days of testimony by Mr. Wende alone, corroborated by multiple other witnesses, 3,500 pages of transcript, and 170,000 pages of corroborating documentary evidence, including bug reports, software release notes, iterative product specifications, schematics, gerber files, and testing data. Moreover, as legal commentators have noted, the factual holding of Suder is inherently limited because ESI was a small company with roughly 125 total employees and 40 engineers, enabling a single operational executive (Mr. Wende) to testify credibly from direct personal knowledge regarding the daily work of the engineering staff. In any larger or multi-site enterprise, a single witness lacks the personal knowledge required to substantiate company-wide percentage allocations without contemporaneous time records.

Second, the lack of project-level time tracking directly threatens compliance with the "substantially all" (80%) process of experimentation fraction under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), which must be applied separately to each business component and measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis. When a taxpayer lacks project-level time tracking (nexus) and one or more projects fail the four-part test—as Chameleon did in Suder—the taxpayer cannot precisely isolate and remove the non-qualifying project's wage costs from the QRE pool; in Suder itself, the Court addressed this only at the aggregate level, extrapolating from the stipulated sample to find that 91.67% (eleven-twelfths) of the 76 projects constituted qualified research and leaving the resulting computations to the parties under Tax Court Rule 155. Even more critically, in the wake of the Seventh Circuit's landmark decision in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), alongside Tax Court rulings in Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, federal courts strictly enforce the 80% fraction at the business-component level. Generalized descriptions of uncertainty, broad assertions of product novelty, and arbitrary estimates of time spent performing experimentation are legally insufficient; if a taxpayer cannot provide a principled, quantitative basis proving that at least 80% of the research activities on a business component constituted elements of a process of experimentation, the entire claim for that component is disallowed.

Third, unsubstantiated C-suite time allocations face near-automatic disallowance under modern jurisprudence. While Mr. Suder's 75% time allocation survived in 2014 because Mr. Boyd managed day-to-day business operations and multiple witnesses corroborated that there was not a single prototype that Mr. Suder had not personally "touched, played with, and blessed" during alpha testing, Tax Court and appellate rulings both before and after Suder—including the earlier decision (distinguished in Suder) in Shami v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-78, and Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, aff'd, 7th Cir. (Apr. 30, 2024)—have disallowed 100% of executive wage QREs where taxpayers relied on general payroll records and oral estimates without objective documentation establishing the exact hours devoted to qualified services.
2.4 Base Period Substantiation Deficiencies and Contract Research Characterization Vulnerabilities

Two additional technical vulnerabilities emerged in the Suder record concerning historical base-period substantiation and third-party expenditure characterization. Under the regular credit calculation method of IRC § 41(a)(1) and (c)(3), a taxpayer must establish its "fixed-base percentage" by proving its aggregate QREs and gross receipts during the statutory base period, and must adhere to the "consistency requirement" of IRC § 41(c)(6) (as in effect for the years at issue in Suder) by defining QREs in the base period consistently with the credit years. In Suder, the Tax Court explicitly noted in its opinion that "there is insufficient evidence in the record for us to compare the projects undertaken by ESI during the base period with the 12 stipulated projects". Although both parties in Suder were deemed to have conceded any consistency-requirement arguments by failing to brief them under Tax Court Rule 151(e), and ESI had already computed its credit using the 16% statutory maximum fixed-base percentage, under federal precedents such as Audio Technica U.S., Inc. v. United States (6th Cir. 2020), a taxpayer's failure to maintain historical base-period records to quantify base-period research expenses and prove consistency can nullify the regular credit entirely or force the taxpayer onto the statutory maximum 16% fixed-base percentage cap (and 50% minimum base amount floor under IRC § 41(c)(2)), severely eroding the net credit. Furthermore, since the IRS's promulgation of rigorous refund claim specificity requirements (requiring identification of all business components, research activities performed, and total qualified wage, supply, and contract research expenses), gaps in project-level and base-period records create immediate administrative rejection risks.

Finally, ESI's characterization of third-party vendor and legal payments highlights a critical distinction between supplies, contract research, and Section 174 patent prosecution costs. ESI claimed contract research expenses ($29,915 in 2004, $15,531 in 2005, $7,755 in 2006, and $10,316 in 2007) for amounts paid to two outside law firms for patent research and patent prosecution, while classifying payments to third-party vendors—including Alta Via for Gerber PCB layout files, Arrow Electronics for electronic components used in prototypes, Avnet Electronics for materials used to assemble circuit boards, and GTECH for manufacturing physical prototype circuit boards—as in-house "supplies" tracked in a dedicated R&D supply account under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). As tax practitioners have noted, the Tax Court held the patent application expenses qualified as contract research QREs "with no analysis," relying on Mr. Wende's credible testimony, the general ledgers introduced for the contract research expenses, and a citation to Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1). In contemporary tax practice, relying on this aspect of Suder is a severe trap: although Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) permits "attorneys' fees expended in making and perfecting a patent application" to be deducted as research and experimental costs under IRC § 174, IRC § 41(b)(3) allows contract research QREs only where a non-employee performs "qualified research" that independently satisfies the technological in nature and scientific process of experimentation tests of IRC § 41(d). Because legal services performed by patent attorneys rely on legal training rather than the physical, biological, engineering, or computer sciences, the IRS routinely disallows patent attorney fees as IRC § 41 contract research QREs outside the Suder record. Moreover, where taxpayers engage in custom engineering contracts without ensuring that payment is strictly contingent on research success and that the taxpayer retains substantial rights in the resulting intellectual property, claims routinely fail under the funded research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), as reinforced by the Eighth Circuit in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), and the Tax Court in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement discussed in Suder v. Commissioner against the taxpayer's specific failure or vulnerability, the Tax Court's standard of proof and holding, and the resulting compliance standard for United States taxpayers.

headers: Taxpayer's Position or Evidentiary Failure in Suder
Tax Court's Standard of Proof, Analysis, & Holding
Strategic Compliance Mandate for U.S. Taxpayers

cells: IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) & Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) (Section 174 Uncertainty Test)
Expenditures must be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business to eliminate uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design at the outset of research.

ESI claimed 76 hardware/software telecom projects (12 stipulated). The IRS challenged all 12 as "routine engineering" or "duplication" lacking uncertainty as to capability, method, or design (relying on an expert report the Court found unreliable).

Standard: Preponderance of evidence showing information available at the outset did not establish capability, method, or appropriate design. Holding: Satisfied for all 12 projects (including Chameleon); in its process-of-experimentation analysis, the Court added that taxpayers are not required to "reinvent the wheel" to establish design or method uncertainty.

Document specific architectural, algorithmic, or electrical design uncertainties at project inception (e.g., PCB signal integrity, NAT traversal, .NET integration) rather than relying on broad assertions of product novelty.
IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)–(ii) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4) (Technological in Nature & Business Component Tests)
Research must fundamentally rely on physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science, and be intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component.

ESI developed embedded PBX systems, PCB cards (DLC0, DLC82, IVC1212), Linux firmware (Pony), and VoIP software (Mad Max). The IRS did not dispute that all 12 projects satisfied the technological information and business component tests.

Standard: Credible technical testimony and design artifacts proving reliance on computer science and electrical engineering principles applied to discrete hardware/software products. Holding: Satisfied (undisputed by the IRS) for all 12 projects.

Define each business component at the discrete product, PCB card, or software module level, and map engineering principles (e.g., C/Assembly firmware, voltage regulation) directly to component specifications.
IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6) (Process of Experimentation & 80% "Substantially All" Test)
At least 80% of research activities per business component must constitute elements of a systematic process of evaluating alternatives (modeling, simulation, systematic trial and error).

The record contained no project-level activity logs quantifying the 80% ratio; ESI relied instead on evidence of its ISO-9000-based multi-phase development lifecycle (Concept → Specs → Prototypes → Alpha/Beta Testing).

Standard: Evidence of a structured, iterative evaluative process testing hypotheses and design alternatives. Holding: 80% threshold met for all 12 projects (bug fixing on commercially ready products was less than 20% of activities), but qualified purpose met for only 11, via multi-iteration specifications, PCB prototypes, smoke/basic/regression tests, and a targeted minimum of 20–25 external beta testers.

In light of post-Suder strictness (Little Sandy Coal, Siemer Milling), do not rely solely on lifecycle narratives; track experimental vs. non-experimental hours per component to prove the ≥80% fraction quantitatively.
IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)–(B) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) (Qualified Purpose, Cosmetic Exclusion, & Shrink-Back Rule)
Experimentation must improve function, performance, reliability, or quality (§ 41(d)(3)(A)); research related to style, taste, or cosmetic design is excluded (§ 41(d)(3)(B)).
Failure: In the Chameleon project, ESI integrated a third-party skinning tool to allow users to change VIP screen colors, fonts, and button shapes/sizes without isolating any functional improvement.

Standard: Proof of functional or performance enhancement; if a whole component fails, proof of a qualifying subset under the shrink-back rule. Holding: Chameleon Disqualified (100%). SVP Wende admitted it did not improve VIP functionality; barred as cosmetic under § 41(d)(3)(B).

Strictly segregate UI/UX aesthetic skinning and style customizations from functional front-end engineering (e.g., rendering latency, memory footprint) into separate subcomponent project codes to preserve shrink-back eligibility.
IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), § 6001, & Cohan Rule (Wage QRE Substantiation & Project "Nexus")
Taxpayers must maintain permanent books and records substantiating wage QREs. Under Cohan, courts may estimate QREs only if qualified research is proven and a reasonable basis exists.
Failure: The opinion describes no contemporaneous time-tracking records linking employee hours to specific projects. SVP Wende estimated annual percentages on Excel spreadsheets.

Standard: Credible testimony from a witness with direct personal knowledge corroborated by extensive documentary evidence. Holding: Rejected IRS project-nexus mandate for wages; accepted Wende's allocations (100% for most engineers, product managers, and testers; generally 5–10% for QC/shipping staff; 25% for Boyd; 75% for the CEO), corroborated by other witnesses and documents, under Cohan after a 3-week trial.

Avoid relying on Cohan estimates, which required 3,500 pages of testimony and 170,000 pages of exhibits to defend in Suder and only worked because ESI had ~40 engineers. Implement contemporaneous project/task time tracking.
IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2) (Executive Qualified Services & 80% Wage Rule)
Wages qualify only for engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research. If ≥80% of an employee's time is qualified, 100% of wages qualify.
CEO Suder claimed 75% of his time as qualified services (intentionally capped below 80% by Wende for conservatism) despite holding a C-suite title and working only 20–30 hours/week.

Standard: Specific proof that the executive personally performed technical ideation, specification review, or hands-on prototype testing rather than general management. Holding: 75% allocation upheld because Boyd ran business operations while Suder led macro-ideation and alpha-tested every prototype.
Document C-suite technical involvement contemporaneously via signed specification approvals, alpha-test logs, and invention disclosures to survive heightened scrutiny under Moore and Shami.
IRC § 174(e) (Reasonableness of Research Compensation)
Research expenditures are eligible as QREs only to the extent that the amount is reasonable under the circumstances.

Failure: ESI paid CEO Suder $8.67M to $10.95M/yr (2/3 of all wage QREs; 4.5x–6x ESI's ordinary business income; ~9:1 ratio to Boyd matching 90/10 stock ownership) and relied on Longnecker's flawed $8.67M–$10.17M royalty valuation.

Standard: Market comparability for actual R&D services rendered, excluding disguised equity distributions and unverified IP royalties. Holding: Found $30.67M of CEO pay unreasonable. Rejected Longnecker's royalty component; capped reasonable pay at Base + Annual + Long-Term Incentive ($2.37M–$2.64M/yr).

Benchmark shareholder-executive W-2 compensation against independent market surveys for technical roles; separate S-corp equity distributions and IP licensing royalties from W-2 wages; document base vs. bonus formulas.
IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) & § 41(b)(3) (Supplies & Contract Research QREs)
Supplies must be tangible property consumed directly in qualified research. Contract research (65%) must be paid to non-employees for qualified research performed on the taxpayer's behalf.

ESI tracked prototype supplies (Alta Via Gerber files, Arrow/Avnet parts, GTECH PCBs) in a dedicated GL account. Claimed fees paid to two law firms for patent research and prosecution as contract research.

Standard: Segregated accounting records and invoices proving direct research consumption or qualifying third-party services. Holding: Supplies and patent prosecution contract research QREs allowed based on Wende's credible testimony, the general ledgers in evidence, and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1).

Maintain a dedicated GL account exclusively for R&D prototype supplies. Exercise extreme caution with patent legal fees: while deductible under IRC § 174, the IRS routinely challenges legal fees under IRC § 41(b)(3) as non-technological.
IRC § 41(c)(1)–(3) (Base Amount & Fixed-Base Percentage Substantiation)
Regular credit requires substantiating historical base-period QREs and gross receipts consistently with credit years (max 16% fixed-base percentage; min 50% base amount floor).
Failure: ESI failed to introduce sufficient historical evidence into the record to allow the Court to compare base-period projects against the 12 stipulated credit-year projects.

Standard: Verifiable historical documentation proving base-period QREs and project consistency. Holding: Both parties were deemed to have conceded any consistency-requirement arguments for failure to brief them (Rule 151(e)); the Court also noted insufficient evidence to compare base-period projects with the 12 stipulated projects, and ESI had used the 16% maximum fixed-base percentage.

If historical base-period project and cost records cannot be substantiated to satisfy the consistency rule, elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC § 41(c)(4) using a rolling 3-year lookback.
IRC § 6662(a) & § 6664(c) (Accuracy-Related Penalties & Good Faith Exception)
20% penalty applies to negligence or substantial understatement unless the taxpayer demonstrates reasonable cause and good faith reliance on competent advisors.

IRS determined 20% accuracy-related penalties in its notices of deficiency; at trial, the penalty analysis addressed the Chameleon disqualification, the wage allocations, and $30.67M in excessive CEO wage QREs.

Standard: Neonatology three-prong reliance test, applied within a case-by-case, facts-and-circumstances determination of reasonable cause and good faith. Holding: No Penalties. Taxpayers were experienced in telephone systems, not tax; they hired Alliantgroup, reasonably entrusted the QRE computations to SVP Wende (for whom it was reasonable to believe Chameleon qualified), and consulted their longtime CPA in setting wages, reflecting an honest, reasonable misunderstanding of the law in a highly complex area where 11 of 12 projects qualified.

Engage qualified, independent R&D tax counsel, provide full and accurate financial/compensation disclosures, and document management's review of the study methodology to preserve IRC § 6664(c) penalty immunity.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of Suder v. Commissioner—and subsequent federal appellate refinements in Little Sandy Coal, Siemer Milling, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, and Moore—into an actionable compliance architecture, the following two applied industry case studies demonstrate step-by-step how United States taxpayers can remediate the exact technical, contractual, compensation, and evidentiary pitfalls exposed in the ruling.
4.1 Case Study 1: Enterprise Telecommunications & SaaS Platform Developer (Overcoming the Cosmetic UI Exclusion, Shrink-Back Failures, and Non-Contemporaneous Nexus Deficiencies)
Industry Scenario & Identified Legal Pitfalls

VoxCore Communications, Inc. ("VoxCore") is a mid-market United States C corporation with 180 employees, including 65 software and network engineers, that develops cloud-hosted Unified Communications as a Service (UCaaS) software and edge-routing appliances for enterprise hospitality clients. For the current tax year, VoxCore plans to claim $1.8 million in federal R&D tax credits across 18 development initiatives. A pre-filing legal audit identifies three critical vulnerabilities that mirror the failures and audit triggers in Suder. First, VoxCore faces the "Chameleon" UI/UX cosmetic trap under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) paired with a shrink-back failure under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). VoxCore's largest initiative, Project Aura ($3.2 million in engineering wages), involves overhauling the company's desktop and mobile softphone application. Roughly 35% of the project's engineering hours were spent integrating an open-source CSS/React theming engine so hotel clients can customize brand logos, color palettes, typography fonts, and button geometry, while the remaining 65% of the hours involved re-architecting the underlying WebRTC client state machine and GPU hardware-acceleration pipeline to eliminate audio jitter and reduce screen-redraw latency by 40 milliseconds during high-concurrency video calls. Because VoxCore tracked all Project Aura work under a single cost center code (PROJ-AURA-01), the 35% cosmetic theming work prevents the overall business component from satisfying the 80% "substantially all" process of experimentation threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), and the absence of subcomponent accounting prevents a court or examiner from applying the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) shrinking-back rule.

Second, like ESI in Suder, VoxCore relies on non-contemporaneous spreadsheet estimates without project nexus, as it does not require its 65 engineers to log time to specific projects. Instead, the VP of Engineering plans to compile a year-end Excel spreadsheet assigning 100% allocations to 50 developers and 50% allocations to 15 DevOps and quality assurance personnel. Unlike ESI's 40-engineer shop overseen by a single hands-on SVP, VoxCore's 65 engineers operate across four remote agile tribes, meaning the VP of Engineering lacks direct personal knowledge of each developer's daily tasks and cannot satisfy the Cohan evidentiary threshold or the Little Sandy Coal 80% component-level proof standard. Third, VoxCore faces characterization and funded-research risks on its third-party contracts: it paid $450,000 to an outside engineering vendor (NexPCB) to generate Gerber files and fabricate 30 alpha-prototype edge-routing appliances, and simultaneously entered into a $1.2 million contract with a major hotel chain (GrandStay) to develop a custom firewall-traversal module (analogous to ESI's Mad Max project) under which GrandStay pays VoxCore monthly progress payments based on engineering hours incurred rather than contingent on technical success.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Business Component Architecture (Proactive Shrink-Back Implementation)

To prevent the 35% cosmetic theming activities from contaminating the 65% WebRTC and GPU performance engineering under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and the 80% "substantially all" rule, VoxCore must restructure its business component taxonomy at the project governance and enterprise resource planning (ERP) levels prior to tax return preparation. Pursuant to IRC § 41(d)(2)(A)–(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), VoxCore must abandon the monolithic Project Aura business component designation and formally partition the initiative into three independent subcomponent business components inside Jira and the general ledger. The first subcomponent, designated BC-AURA-WEBRTC, encompasses the WebRTC Media Engine and Jitter-Buffer State Machine, undertaken for the qualified purpose of improving audio and video packet reliability and network performance under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A). The second subcomponent, designated BC-AURA-RENDER, encompasses the Client GPU Hardware-Acceleration and DOM Virtualization Engine, undertaken for the qualified purpose of improving UI frame-rate performance and reducing CPU memory consumption under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A). The third subcomponent, designated BC-AURA-THEME, isolates the White-Label CSS/React Skinning and Aesthetic Customization Module, which relates to style, taste, and cosmetic design factors under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B). By isolating BC-AURA-THEME into its own tracking code and voluntarily excluding 100% of its hours from the QRE claim, VoxCore ensures that within the remaining BC-AURA-WEBRTC and BC-AURA-RENDER business components, over 92% of the engineering activities constitute a rigorous process of experimentation for a qualified functional purpose—surpassing the 80% "substantially all" mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) without relying on a court to retroactively apply the shrink-back rule.
Step 2: Technical Documentation of Technological Uncertainty and the Process of Experimentation

To capitalize on Suder's holding that taxpayers need not "reinvent the wheel" while surviving post-Siemer Milling and Phoenix Design Group scrutiny requiring empirical proof of the scientific method, VoxCore must embed mandatory technical documentation gates into its software development lifecycle (SDLC). Before sprint coding commences on BC-AURA-WEBRTC or the firewall-traversal module, the lead software architect must execute a standardized Technical Uncertainty & Architecture Decision Record (ADR) that explicitly documents why publicly available knowledge, standard WebRTC specifications, or existing open-source libraries cannot achieve the target packet-loss recovery threshold across asymmetric enterprise NAT firewalls, thereby establishing capability, method, or appropriate design uncertainty at the outset of research under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1). Each ADR must further log at least two competing technical alternatives evaluated by the engineering team—such as comparing Forward Error Correction (FEC) with dynamic Reed-Solomon coding against Selective Retransmission (NACK) with predictive Kalman-filter jitter buffering—and state the testable hypothesis for each alternative to satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5). Throughout development, VoxCore must archive automated CI/CD unit test outputs, smoke and regression test logs, packet-capture simulation data, alpha-test failure reports, and beta-test telemetry from its 25 external hospitality beta sites, creating an empirical record of systematic trial, data analysis, hypothesis refinement, and retesting prior to commercial release.
Step 3: Re-Engineering Experimentation Tracking and Cost-to-Project Nexus

To eliminate reliance on the perilous Cohan estimation rule and satisfy the quantitative substantiation standards of IRC § 6001 and Little Sandy Coal, VoxCore must replace year-end management spreadsheets with automated, bi-directional SDLC time-and-activity tracking integrated directly with its Agile development sprints and Git commits. Every Jira story, task, and bug ticket must require two mandatory metadata fields before a developer can merge a Git pull request: Business_Component_ID (mapping to the specific subcomponent) and R&D_Activity_Classification. The R&D_Activity_Classification field must categorize logged hours into four precise statutory buckets: Code E1 for direct experimentation (architecture modeling, algorithm coding, prototype integration, and pre-release alpha/beta testing and debugging); Code E2 for direct supervision and direct support (first-line technical code reviews, specification sign-offs, and test-environment setup directly supporting Code E1); Code N1 for non-experimental research activity on the component (routine data migration or third-party API boilerplate configuration, which enters the denominator of the 80% test but is excluded from the numerator); and Code X1 for excluded post-production and maintenance work (bug fixing on commercially available software versions, routine quality control, and general administrative meetings, which are completely excluded from the credit calculation, mirroring Mr. Wende's exclusion of non-sporadic maintenance in Suder). At the close of each two-week agile sprint, the ERP system must aggregate each engineer's logged ticket hours across E1, E2, N1, and X1 and capture a digital attestation from both the engineer and their first-line engineering manager, creating permanent books and records under Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1 that mathematically validate the ≥80% process-of-experimentation fraction for every business component.
Step 4: Restructuring Third-Party Vendor and Customer Contracts

Finally, VoxCore must restructure its external vendor and customer agreements to protect its supply QREs and prevent disqualification under the funded research exclusion. Following the successful accounting practice in Suder—where ESI's payments to Alta Via for Gerber files, Arrow for electronic components and Avnet for circuit-board assembly materials, and GTECH for prototype PCBs were upheld as supplies on the basis of SVP Wende's credible testimony and the general ledger for the single account he used exclusively for R&D supplies—VoxCore must establish a segregated general ledger account (GL-5410: R&D Prototype Supplies) requiring engineering sign-off. The purchase order with NexPCB must explicitly stipulate that NexPCB is fabricating tangible prototype circuit boards strictly to VoxCore's engineering drawings, and that all 30 units are non-depreciable experimental "pilot models" under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) that will be consumed or destroyed during internal alpha and external beta stress testing rather than held for commercial sale, thereby qualifying 100% of the $450,000 expenditure as in-house supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). Simultaneously, to prevent the GrandStay firewall-traversal project from being disqualified as "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson (8th Cir. 2024), VoxCore must execute a formal contract amendment prior to performing the research that replaces hourly progress billing with a fixed-price, milestone-contingent fee structure. The amended contract must explicitly state that payment is contingent upon the success of the research—requiring the firewall-traversal module to pass quantifiable technical acceptance testing, with a binding contractual and state-law obligation to refund advances if VoxCore fails to deliver a functioning solution—and must expressly vest sole ownership of all underlying source code, patents, and substantial intellectual property rights in VoxCore, granting GrandStay only a non-exclusive license to use the resulting software.

4.2 Case Study 2: Closely Held Hardware & Embedded Systems S-Corporation (Overcoming IRC Section 174(e) Executive Compensation Disallowance, Direct Supervision Substantiation, and Base Period Failures)
Industry Scenario & Identified Legal Pitfalls

VoltEdge MicroSystems, Inc. ("VoltEdge") is a closely held Texas S corporation with 95 employees, including 32 electrical and firmware engineers, that designs and manufactures high-density, low-voltage industrial power-distribution and telemetry circuit boards analogous to ESI's Phoenix, DLC0, DLC82, and IVC1212 projects. VoltEdge is owned 85% by its founder and CEO, Dr. Marcus Vance, and 15% by its COO, Sarah Sterling. For the current tax year, VoltEdge intends to claim $11.5 million in total QREs, generating substantial flow-through research tax credits on the personal returns of Dr. Vance and Ms. Sterling. A pre-audit legal review uncovers four severe compliance failures directly parallel to Suder. First, VoltEdge faces a massive unreasonable compensation disallowance under IRC § 174(e). In the current tax year, VoltEdge reported $2.1 million in ordinary corporate net income after paying Dr. Vance $9,350,000 in W-2 wages and Ms. Sterling $1,650,000 in W-2 wages. Their compensation consists of an undocumented blend of base salary and year-end cash flow bonuses paid in an exact 85:15 ratio (5.67:1) matching their equity ownership split, with Dr. Vance's pay equaling 4.45 times corporate net income. VoltEdge plans to allocate 80% of Dr. Vance's wages (or 100% under the "substantially all" wage rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), totaling $9,350,000) to qualified services based on a compensation consultant's memo attributing $6.8 million of Dr. Vance's pay to "implied founder patent royalties."

Second, Dr. Vance's qualified services allocation is unsubstantiated under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Moore v. Commissioner (7th Cir. 2024): he works a variable schedule of roughly 25 hours per week, maintains no calendar logs or time records, has not been named as an inventor on a new patent application in four years, and relies solely on an oral assertion that he spends 80% of his working hours guiding product vision and testing prototypes. Third, VoltEdge included $180,000 paid to an outside intellectual property law firm for prior-art searches, patent application drafting, and USPTO office-action responses as IRC § 41(b)(3) contract research expenses. Fourth, VoltEdge faces a fatal base-period substantiation failure under IRC § 41(c)(3): founded in 1991, the company intends to claim the Regular Research Credit using a 3.5% historical fixed-base percentage, but due to an accounting system purge in 2012, it possesses zero project records or general ledger payroll details from its historical base period to prove consistency with current-year projects.
Step 1: Restructuring Corporate Governance and Executive Compensation Architecture Under IRC § 174(e)

To prevent an IRS examination from disallowing 75% or more of Dr. Vance's claimed wage QREs under IRC § 174(e)—as occurred in Suder—and to insulate the shareholders against 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a), VoltEdge must immediately overhaul its corporate compensation and distribution governance. VoltEdge's Board of Directors must adopt a formal Executive Compensation & Shareholder Distribution Charter that strictly decouples W-2 compensation for personal services rendered under IRC § 3401(a) from S-corporation shareholder distributions with respect to stock. Year-end distributions of residual corporate cash flow that track the 85%/15% stock ownership ratio must be declared and reported exclusively as non-wage shareholder distributions on Schedule K-1, eliminating the exact proportionate wage-to-stockholding ratio that triggered close judicial scrutiny in Suder.

Furthermore, tax counsel must instruct VoltEdge to reject any compensation study that embeds hypothetical gross-revenue or patent royalties inside W-2 wages, as the Tax Court in Suder flatly rejected royalty-based compensation models as unverified and legally ineligible for QRE inclusion. Instead, VoltEdge must commission an independent executive compensation valuation benchmarking Dr. Vance's pay against the 75th to 90th percentile of Chief Technology Officers and R&D-focused Chief Executives at comparable electronics manufacturers, structured explicitly into the three compensation components validated by Judge Vasquez in Suder: a documented Base Salary ($460,000, explicitly calibrated to reflect Dr. Vance's 25-hour-per-week schedule); an Annual Technical Performance Incentive ($440,000, tied by pre-set board resolution to objective engineering milestones such as passing alpha and beta validation on three new 3.3V surface-mount PCB designs rather than raw corporate cash flow); and a Long-Term R&D Incentive Plan ($1,650,000, tied to multi-year product commercialization and hardware reliability metrics). Even if VoltEdge elects to pay Dr. Vance more than this $2,550,000 total in W-2 payroll, the company must self-impose the $2,550,000 IRC § 174(e) reasonable compensation cap on Form 6765 before applying his qualified services allocation percentage.
Step 2: Contemporaneous Substantiation of C-Suite Technical Ideation and Direct Supervision Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)

To ensure that Dr. Vance's qualified time allocation survives both Suder scrutiny and the stringent post-Moore and Shami substantiation requirements, VoltEdge cannot rely on an undocumented 75% or 80% estimate. Corporate resolutions and executive job descriptions must formally establish that COO Sarah Sterling exercises sole responsibility over day-to-day business administration, finance, human resources, and commercial sales, while Dr. Vance's mandate is dedicated to serving as Chief Product Architect and Director of Alpha Testing—replicating the Boyd/Suder operational division of labor that the Court found in the record of Suder. Because Dr. Vance works a variable 25-hour schedule, he must maintain a contemporaneous digital calendar and engineering sign-off registry logging his exact hours across four verifiable technical activities: attendance rosters and whiteboard schematics from weekly 1.5-to-2-hour macro-feasibility ideation meetings with senior electrical engineers; version-controlled PDFs of functional and design specifications bearing Dr. Vance's digital signature, timestamp, and technical redlines prior to project codename approval; a structured Alpha Prototype Bench-Test Log documenting his physical inspection, oscilloscope signal-integrity testing, and firmware verification of every prototype PCB prior to external beta release; and documented 1-on-1 technical troubleshooting sessions directly supervising senior engineers on power-isolation and trace-termination challenges. At year-end, dividing Dr. Vance's contemporaneously logged technical hours (910 hours) by his total logged working hours (1,300 hours) yields a precise, audit-proof 70.0% qualified services allocation applied against his $2,550,000 reasonable compensation cap ($1,785,000 in substantiated wage QREs).
Step 3: Segregating Patent Prosecution Expenses from Qualifying R&D Activities

To eliminate audit exposure regarding the $180,000 paid to outside patent counsel, VoltEdge must align its tax reporting with the statutory boundary between IRC § 174 and IRC § 41(b)(3). Although the Tax Court in Suder permitted fees paid to two law firms for patent research and prosecution to be included as contract research QREs without substantive analysis by citing Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), relying on that anomaly in an IRS examination is hazardous because legal services performed by patent attorneys do not fundamentally rely on engineering or computer science or constitute a scientific process of experimentation under IRC § 41(b)(3) and § 41(d)(1)(B)–(C). VoltEdge should, as a conservative position that goes beyond what Suder required, reclassify the $180,000 in outside law firm invoices out of its Form 6765 contract research QRE pool and instead treat those patent perfection fees strictly as Section 174/174A research and experimental expenditures. Conversely, all hours spent by Dr. Vance and VoltEdge's internal electrical engineers conducting experimental lab tests, generating empirical signal-integrity plots, and drafting technical schematic disclosures to support new patent applications should be contemporaneously logged and claimed as in-house wage QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), which simultaneously reinforces the reasonableness of Dr. Vance's technical compensation under IRC § 174(e).
Step 4: Remediating Base Period Substantiation via the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) Election

Finally, to resolve VoltEdge's inability to substantiate its 1990s historical base-period projects and prevent a complete credit disallowance under the consistency rule of IRC § 41(c)(6) (as in effect for the years at issue in Suder)—or a fallback to the maximum 16% fixed-base percentage that ESI itself used in Suder—VoltEdge must modify its statutory calculation election. On its timely filed original federal Form 6765, VoltEdge must abandon the Regular Research Credit and formally elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC § 41(c)(4), which calculates the credit as 14% of the excess of credit-year QREs over 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years. Because the ASC method eliminates any requirement to substantiate historical 1980s or 1990s base-period gross receipts or decades-old project consistency, VoltEdge only needs to substantiate its QREs across the immediately preceding three-year rolling lookback period, for which the company possesses complete ERP payroll records, PCB prototype supply invoices, and engineering specifications. By consistently applying the independent IRC § 174(e) reasonable compensation cap to Dr. Vance's wages across both the three lookback years and the current credit year, rather than using current-year QREs to retroactively estimate past years, VoltEdge satisfies the base-period substantiation and consistency mandates of IRC § 41(c), securing a fully defensible R&D tax credit claim while preserving complete penalty protection under IRC § 6664(c).
